item.title: Your Agents Ship Fast. Make Them Pass a Release Gate First
item.description: Before tagging ai-finance-coach 1.0.0, one command found my first name in a test, an employer in a test id and one of my own figures in the demo data, all in a repository with green CI. What leaks when agents work with real data, why CI and secret scanners can’t see it, and the generic recipe I use now - one scripted release gate, a local term file that never enters the repository, and four places that force everyone, agents included, to run it.

item.title: Six Weeks in One Night: How a Product Gets Built in the Agentic Era
item.description: I gave a human development plan to a team of agents, an Opus spec writer, a Sonnet developer and an Opus reviewer, and let them build the first phase of Graft overnight. Six planned weeks became one night, at about 0.5% of the human cost. But the bottleneck didn’t disappear. It moved to us.

item.title: You Don't Need a Scion: Graft, a Review Layer for Agent Pull Requests
item.description: Anthropic’s Scion solves a storage problem only a few companies have. The workflow problem behind it, too many agent pull requests for the humans who review them, is everyone’s. Graft, now public, puts a checked intent card, a risk class no model can lower and a policy verdict on every pull request, so reviewers read the card before the diff. What ships in v0.0.1, how a reviewer’s day changes, the video, and what the live test checks.

item.title: Use AI to Build the Tool, Not to Be the Tool
item.description: Asking an agent to block focus time, summarise yesterday’s numbers or find a meeting slot works, but you pay for it every time, and the answer changes. I measured 14 Claude Code runs on three everyday jobs. Writing the script once costs about as much as asking once. With an interactive calculator, a checklist, and my own projects as examples.

item.title: Drowning in Email: ai-email-assistant, Rules First, Models Last
item.description: A Gmail triage that costs cents. Deterministic rules handle the routine mail, Claude Haiku looks only at what’s left, Claude Sonnet only at what Haiku isn’t sure about, and code validates every answer. Requests become Google Tasks with a due date. With a real run on my inbox, a from-zero install with Homebrew, and a few thoughts on letting an AI answer your mail.

item.title: New Week, Another AI Coach: ai-finance-coach
item.description: A self-hosted coach for your household’s money. PSD2 bank sync through Enable Banking, an encrypted local database, a one-time login link or a passkey, and a language model that only ever receives redacted, pseudonymised, already computed figures. With real examples of what stays on your machine and what is sent.

item.title: Narrated Product Videos Without a Video File: a Canvas, JavaScript and a Free Voice-Over
item.description: A video that is a web page: frames drawn in JavaScript, a free synthetic voice, an agent doing the heavy lifting. The method, every free TTS option worth knowing (and which ones you are actually allowed to publish), and a step-by-step example you can watch right here.

item.title: ai-running-coach, Five Days Later: a Chat, a Gear Locker, a GPS Map and a Video Series
item.description: A chat with the coach inside the dashboard, a GPS map on every session, a calorie model that checks Garmin’s numbers, a full gear locker with photo inspections, running dynamics, a second contributor, and “The Trail”, a video series drawn in JavaScript that you can watch right here.

item.title: ai-running-coach, Nine Days Later: a Dashboard, 20+ Metrics and a Coach in My Pocket
item.description: A dashboard, a pile of new metrics, guardrails that can say no, and a coach that lives on a Linux box at home and answers me from my phone. Here is what changed in ai-running-coach since the ultra, and why the automatic sync runs on cron instead of a Claude routine.

item.title: system-one-router: Letting a "System One" Model Pick the Right LLM for Every Prompt
item.description: My first model router let an LLM read a prompt file and pick an agent. This one asks a “System One” decision model four typed questions, scores the models with plain arithmetic, and publishes a benchmark to prove it works (and to show where it doesn’t).
